And a commitment to serve, to protect dignity, and to hold on to hope, even in the most difficult times or difficult chapters. Every word I share today comes from the lived reality, not from a paper or policy brief or headline, but from what we see and feel every day and working on the ground in a place where space for women keeps shrinking. I meet women who are part of our initiatives and they have no other support other than us. And the grassroots organizations that women lead and are part of and the whole still find ways to operate regardless of the many bans placed on us. Even through everything we have faced, women-led organizations have not stopped, and we have remained close to our communities, responding with care, with trust, with persistence. In a place where others cannot go, we are already present. In homes where silence has replaced voices, we create spaces to speak. And in the systems that have left women behind, we still try to serve them in any way we can. One of the few enablers that have helped us continue our work has been the support from various donors. This support does not only provide essential supplies, it's also keep the local organizations alive. For example, the AHF, the Afghanistan Humanitarian Fund, has enabled us to pay our staff, sustain safe space for work, respond rapidly during emergencies. Also, the UN agencies, like UN Women, support us in critical time and have helped build our technical capacity and amplify our voices in key spaces. One year ago, I would never have thought that I would be with you here today, addressing this important forum and giving my perspective as an Afghan woman leader. When Under-Secretary-General visited Kabul recently, we appreciate not just his presence, but that he listened. And we share what I want to emphasize again here today. Afghan women are still here. We are not just recipients. We are responders and leaders. And the decision made in global rooms like this deeply affected what is possible back home. And I also want to highlight something very important, the rule of gender focus structures in humanitarian work. Two in particular, the Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, the GHA, and the Women's Advisory Group, WAG. Both of them are helping ensuring that women's voices and needs are not left behind. Like the WAGG has created a spaces for women from across the countries to share their perspectives. And the GEHA group has helped push for principled, inclusive programming and real gender mainstreaming, not just in words, but in action. I think if these spaces disappear, if gender becomes a secondary issue, then women and girls will once again be invisible in planning and response. That's a risk we cannot afford. And we also need to continue shifting power toward localization and women-led organizations. And that's not what we are not asking to be included. We are already doing the work. And what we need is trust, flexible funding, meaningful partnership, and this kind of. I come here not just to speak, but to affirm something also. Like the Afghan women in Afghanistan are still working with courage. That local actors, all of them still responding with the current consistency. And that our continued partnership, your continued partnership, allow us to keep going. Also, let me close with something I often hear from the women we serve. They often say this to me, like, we don't need someone to save us. We just need the chance to save ourselves. So I ask this, if we believe in solidarity, let's act on it. If we believe humanitarian response should be local, let's fund local actors directly. And if we believe in dignity for all, let's walk with women. Even the road is hard. And I don't want to speak more. and get a time. I wanted to thank you so much for standing with us, everyone who's in this global gathering. Thank you so much for standing with us. Thank you for giving us the moments to share our thoughts. Thank you very much.

I thank the director of Ceyan for joining us today. We will now hear from Mr. Amjad Shawa. Mr. Shawa is the director of the Palestinian NGO Network and has decades of experience as a humanitarian and human rights advocate. Mr. Shawa, you have the floor. Would you please unmute yourself? We cannot listen.

Thank you. Excellencies and colleagues, thanks for giving me this opportunity to speak to you today directly from Gaza, a place suffering under a brutal Israeli genocide and blockade for over 20 months. But just to start as you started, Your Excellency, to talk about children, about a child called Ahmed Zidan, 12 years old boy from Khan Yunis. Ahmed's mother, Reem, left home one morning to collect food from the so-called Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, GHF, distribution point in Rafah, despite the danger. She had no choice. Her children were starving. Ahmed walked beside her for hours under the threat of gunfire. As they approached the area, shots rang out. People screamed and ran. Then, Ahmed saw his mother fall, hit by a bullet. For hours, he stayed beside her body. unable to leave while bullets flew around him. Eventually, he was forced to leave her behind to find help. This wasn't the first loss for Ahmed. His brother, Nabil, has already been killed in Israeli airstrike the last year. Ahmed has dreams as yours. Dreams to have peaceful globe. No wars, no killing. What should be aid centers have become death traps. Civilians risk their lives for food only to be shot, tear gassed, or humiliated. Ahmed's plea is simple. dignity, and protection. He wants food, but not at the cost of his mother's life. Yesterday, only yesterday, there was 70 people were killed while they were waiting for aid trucks. Part of them in the so-called Gaza Humanitarian Foundation military distribution points. I speak to you today from Gaza, where starvation has become official policy. Since March 2025, almost no aid has entered Gaza Strip. And the result, 71,000 children now face acute malnutrition. 60 children have died from starvation since March. Pregnant women suffer anemia rates above 60%. This is not a crisis. It's a genocide by design. And yet, in this darkness, Palestinian civil society, which is proud of the partnership with the colleagues of the UN agencies, INGOs, this civil society has been Gaza's lifeline under the bombardment and the blockade. We continue to work to have community kitchens, mobile clinics, and learning spaces. We reach the most vulnerable, newborns in the overcrowded shelters, people with disability unable to flee, children with chronic illness, pregnant women lacking care, the elder trapped under troubles, and orphans who are left behind. All guided by the humanitarian principles, mainly do no harm principle. We have lost hundreds of our colleagues, the aid workers. We do commemorate their lives. And still we are losing. Almost every day, we are losing part of these heroes on the ground. From UNRWA only, we have 280 aid workers who were killed. Gaza health system and water system are collapsing. Of the 55,000 people who are killed, 70% are women and children. Nearly half of them are under age 15. We demand you to work for actions, for a permanent ceasefire, for sanctions on those using starvation as a weapon, for those who are trying to replace our principles, our humanitarian principles, with such military mechanisms. We urge you to work to open all the crossing now to enter this blocked aid, 130,000 tons of aid is blocked for months. We urge you to work for justice for the victims, for these children who lost their mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters. End all military aid and arms transfer fueling this war. The humanitarian system cannot be reformed with more task forces and pledges, while enabling policies of starvation and siege. From Palestine to Sudan, Myanmar to Haiti, civil society is telling you the same thing. Center justice. Support those who have legitimacy on the ground. Gaza, not in need only for your statements and concerns. We need you to act. When history will judge this moment, we'll remember your courage, not your complicity. Please, don't fail Ahmeds and Gaza children anymore. Thank you.

I thank the director of the Palestinian NGO Network. Excellencies, colleagues, as we have heard, the humanitarian challenges ahead are enormous. While remaining grounded in humanitarian principles, we need a revitalized system guided by the people it serves that is smaller, smarter, and sharper. In the coming days, we will explore what this means in more detail. The four panels we have on the humanitarian reset, respect for international humanitarian law, adapting financing for an effective and efficient response, and looking at innovative models to save lives, reduce suffering, and promote people's resilience. We will hear from representatives from national and local organizations here in person and by remote for these important discussions. Your perspectives and contributions are invaluable. I expect our discussions to help us identify and rally around opportunities to reinforce and strengthen the coordination of humanitarian assistance in support of people in need globally. Thank you. I will now briefly pause the meeting to allow the podium to be rearranged. High Level Panel 1 will begin momentarily. Please remain seated. Colleagues, please find your seats. We will now begin high level panel one on the humanitarian reset, a dialogue with principles on the future of humanitarian action. It is my pleasure to welcome you to our first high level panel. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, we gather for what may be the most consequential dialogue on humanitarian action in two decades since landmark changes in 2005. Those changes, spurred by lessons from crises in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Darfur, and later the Indian Ocean tsunami, are chief enduring innovations. The cluster system for accountability, the strengthened humanitarian coordinator functions for coordination, and the transformation of a modest local facility into the robust Central Emergency Response Fund. These changes brought significant improvements in the scale and predictability of humanitarian assistance, yet the context has fundamentally changed. The number of conflicts, has multiplied as political solutions have grown scarce, climate change effects have intensified, disregard for the laws of war have worsened suffering. Over the past decade, the number of people in need has grown steadily and rapidly. while the generosity of donors could no longer keep pace with demands for humanitarian assistance. Few of us could have predicted just how large, swift, and dramatic funding cuts would become. As Under-Secretary-General and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher stated in our recent briefing, "People are dying right now because of aid cuts." Therefore, unlike in 2005, the humanitarian reset represents nothing less than a revolution in how we conceive, organize, and deliver humanitarian assistance. Mr. Fletcher has outlined a reset built on three R's: regroup, reform, and renew. With renewal resting on four pillars: define, deliver, devolve, and defend. This framework challenges to fundamentally reimagine humanitarian action for the realities of today and tomorrow. Today, dialogues will be courageously frank. We see honest assessments from humanitarian principles on the future of a system that must put people in need first. Our principles will address how the sector must adapt to current operational, political, economic, and financial challenges within the RESETS framework. It will explore critical questions. What is needed? Where are the gaps? What can be improved, including in seeking efficiencies? How can the sector become lighter and more effective, both immediately and in the longer term? The discussion will examine how humanitarian organizations should navigate a shifting global order and the rising influence of different actors in conflict areas. We will address how to build coherence among partners and between headquarters and field operations. Our panelists represent the diversity and strength of the humanitarian system. They bring perspective from different organizations, regions, and operational contexts. Each has confronted the challenges we will discuss in different ways. Their insights will inform not only today's conversation, but the strategic direction of humanitarian action as we move forward. They understand that the status quo is unsustainable and that transformation, however difficult, is essential. I'm pleased to welcome our distinguished speakers. I also welcome Mr. Jeremy Bonynge, who will be moderating today's panel following the initial intervention. We shall now hear presentations by our distinguished panelists. I would like, I would now like to turn to Mr. Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator at the Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, OCHA. Tom, simply put, what is your vision for the humanitarian reset? Can you elaborate on the four pillars, define, deliver, devolve, and defend? and what this looks like for people in need and for humanitarians. Over to you.

Thank you, Madam Vice President, and I pay tribute again to your extraordinary work on this call to action and bringing us together today. I'll be very brief at this point because many of you have already heard from me already this morning, but also you've heard much more powerfully from Noor, from Saha, from Amjad, why this moment matters. the context that we face as a global community right now. But also because you'll hear from my much more eloquent colleagues, and we're all part of a community right now. We have different logos and egos and acronyms, but we're all working to a common mission and a common purpose. I don't know if we can quite start and finish each other's sentences, but we can get pretty close. And so I really want to leave as much time as possible for them. but also as much time to hear from all of you because we are acting on your instructions. We are representing you out there in this more transactional, less generous world, and we need your support, as I've said earlier. So, we've set direction on these three phases of the reset. I won't test you on what they are, but it is, of course, regroup, reform, and renew. The IASC met yesterday in the wonderful offices of the IFRC to really focus on those first two, really, the regrouping and the reform parts. And if you hear nothing else today-- actually, there's one other thing I want you to hear in a moment. But if you hear nothing else today, please hear this, we have a plan. And I will spare you all the elements of it. I'll give you a couple of highlights of it now, and I will share more in public in the next couple of days on the detail of that plan. But we really have started to deliver those phases of regroup and reform. It's happening already, a third coming out of the sector as we remove a lot of duplication, bureaucracy, as we really focus on those that we serve. Building though on years of extraordinary work and confidence that we know how to do this. We are not regrouping because we've suddenly decided we weren't doing a good job. We are regrouping under the savage pressure of brutal and rapid cuts to our work. So what are we doing right now? There's a mindset shift. We are doing all we can to remove turf wars. between agencies, between UN and NGOs, between international NGOs and local NGOs, really focusing relentlessly on the bottom line of who does what uniquely well, and let's do that. We are moving in all our conversations, not from observing problems to trying to fix problems, to really being as practical as we can, and from shifting from a system based on the money we wished we had and that we hope we will get to one based on the money that we can realistically secure and how we will deliver that in the most prioritised way possible. A system which will be local where possible, international only when necessary, shared where possible and alone only when necessary and bottom up, not top down. And all of us in the sector all of us will be asking ourselves what power do we have and how can we share it what can be done better by the communities we serve than by us so to answer your question vice president and again only very briefly on the four D's they define We have launched this week our hyper-prioritized global humanitarian overview. And I don't do that with any joy or relish. We've already prioritized 190 million of the 307 million people that we should be reaching if this was a sane world. And now we're reducing that further to the 114 million people we could reach this year if, and this is the second thing I really want you to report back to your capitals, And I've said it already, but if your colleague has written this down in the report of the first session, please put it in bold in the report that goes back. Please underline it in the report that goes, put it in the title, please, of the report that goes back to capitals. We are only asking for 1% as the global humanitarian community to reach those 114 million people. We're asking for 1%. of what we collectively spent on defence last year. One percent of what the world spent on defence last year. Surely, surely we can do that. Surely that resonates with our politicians and most importantly with our public. Then the work strand around deliver, which includes empowering our humanitarian country teams, making sure that they've got more resource and more authority, but also making sure that there is a clear compact with them that they will really deliver for those we serve. We are looking to share services by default across the UN family and beyond. Supply chains, back offices, communication, logistics as far as possible. We're looking to shift towards multipurpose use of cash where it's appropriate and where we can see it works. We will ensure, as I underlined earlier, that protection of women and girls is at the heart of the humanitarian reset, not just protection, but the leadership of women and girls is at the heart of the humanitarian reset. And we say that, and this was unequivocally clear from the IASC meeting yesterday, in a moment when we recognize the challenges, the increased challenges faced by women and girls in this moment of change and flux. We'll deliver with more anticipatory action, and we will deliver in a way that retains this essential link between humanitarian and development work until the point where we don't have to talk about that anymore. I, for one, am sick of talking about the resilience and nexus and so on. Let's just get on and do it. Show, not tell, that this matters to us. But we'll also deliver a green humanitarian reset, sustainability at the heart of it, and we'll find ways to use new technology, and Amy and others are really on the cutting edge of this, to make sure that we work more effectively in the future. We will, the third D, devolve I've talked a bit about how we devolve authority to leadership in country, the humanitarian country teams, making sure that the coordination models are more context specific, more driven by local priorities, by the communities in which they are rooted, finding different ways to hold us to account and involve those voices of local communities in those accountability models, shift more money towards pooled funds, and again towards local actors within those pooled funds, particularly, I think, we think, an emphasis on women-led organisations. And we will streamline the cluster system that has grown up around our work, much of which is essential and very useful, but where there has been a bit too much growth, and we think we can halve the numbers, the number of clusters that support our work. And then constantly seek to improve our funds, the emergency fund, the central emergency fund and others to ensure they are really delivering the support that you ask us to deliver. And then the final D and I'll close here is, is defend where the strongest message out of the IASC meeting yesterday was that we really have to hold the line We must defend this space around international humanitarian law. It is not just the money which is under attack at the moment. It is the values at the heart of what we do. And we heard about many of the crisis contexts where that challenge is most acute. And we are determined as a collective, as a humanitarian community, to hold that line and defend that space unequivocally. through our advocacy, through our campaigns, and through working with all of you to hold that space. So we hope that this plan, these different elements, add up to a bold reimagination of the humanitarian system, drawing on the best of the work that we've done, the confidence from what we've delivered in the past. but also this sense that we will continue to change and innovate and grow with always those we serve at the very, very heart of the mission. And we need your support as the global humanitarian community, as member states, not just to help us secure that funding. And again, I underline, we're not asking for the moon here, but also to back us on the values and to bring your voice to this collective effort. And so I very much look forward to hearing from colleagues, hearing from you, and to a very rich discussion this morning. Thank you.

I thank Mr. Fleischer for elaborating on the four pillars. And I would like to turn now to Mr. Jagan Chabagane, Secretary General of the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent. Jagan, what do you hope will be key elements of the approach to humanitarian work after the reset?

Thank you. Thank you, Madam Vice Chair. Thank you, Tom, for that great introduction and wonderful speech earlier. And on your question, of course, you heard a lot on the sort of the more collective reset that Tom had been talking about in the morning and just now. I would like to share a perspective from IFRC, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. Already late last year, we had initiated a process of listening, even before the current funding crisis became so prominent. Because what we believe is that it's extremely important for the organizations to have that humility on a regular basis to have that check that whether we are up to date or not. It's not about being good or bad. I think as Red Cross, I believe we have always been very good, but there are always opportunity to gain efficiency, cost effectiveness, and the reach of our program. And as part of that process, we have listened to more than 2,000 voices, more than half of them from the local communities. And there are few ideas emerging which very much aligns with the reset process we have been discussing more broadly as a humanitarian sector. One of the first things that came out from that is that the humanitarian system after the reset would be very local. And But it is local with accountability. And the accountability, not in the sense of just pushing the risks to the local actors, but sharing the risks, but delivering in an accountable manner. And it's all, it's really about the decision making at the local level. And I think the colleague from Afghanistan, what she said is that, you don't need to push us forward, we're already there. And somehow we have this notion that we need to put the local actor in the front. No, they're already there. We need to follow them. And I think we need to have the courage to follow the local actors who are already there. And also, we do need, while, you know, as IFC, we have been championing the localization, we also believe that the global solidarity is needed in many, many places. But when we do that global solidarity, I think it's really, really important that now we walk the talk, both the donors community and us as the international organization. We committed 25% of the internationally mobilized funding that goes to the local actors. We have achieved only 2% collectively. That must not be good enough for us, otherwise we'll keep on talking. And this is in our hand to change that. Nobody is stopping us to make that happen. So let's make that happen. And just to share with you colleagues that in the IFC, we are going to set up that target to 75%. We will not be satisfied with 25%. That's the push we want to make. Now, the second message that is coming is, I think the humanitarian system and as an organization, I think we got to have more collaboration, as you said, Tom, no silos, no egos. But at the same time, we also need to be much more conscious about our own mission creeps. Sometimes we establish complicated coordination mechanism, and maybe those were not needed if we are not doing the mission creep ourselves. We do mission creeps and it becomes complicated. We overlap each other, then we create a complicated mechanism to say that, oh, actually, we should not be doing the mission creep. So I think we need that focus, humanitarian focus, and really, really be disciplined ourselves so that the Tom's life becomes very easy and maybe not needed. I think if we can make Tom's job redundant, we would have succeeded. And we do need to diversify our financing approaches and models. And I think in IFRC, we are taking some really innovative financing modalities, but we have to take it to scale. Third one is a real issue around the humanitarian diplomacy, around how we preserve our humanitarian space, how do we protect our humanitarian workers, how do we uphold our principles and the international norms. And I think collectively, again, we have to push for this. And from the, so our call to the government is, as the states, I think you really have to uphold your friends accountable as much as you do to your foes. I think the current system, the system jumps very much to hold your foes accountable, not always your friends accountable. And for me, until and unless we have the courage to help our friends accountable, we will not overcome the sense of impunity that we are seeing around the world. And I think the discipline that we need from the humanitarian workers is that we should not pretend to be replacing the responsibility of the states. Most of the crisis we are seeing now and the pressure on the humanitarian organization is growing because there haven't been many political solutions to many of the crisis we are dealing with now. Until and unless there are political solutions to this crisis, the humanitarians, even if we get 200 billion, Tom, we will not be able to address those issues. There must be political solutions. Now, the fourth is we are also living in a digital age. So I think we as an organization, the humanitarian system, will also have to adopt the digitalization and ethical adoption of artificial intelligence. And this, my son asked me to put, he is artificial intelligence student. And then finally, finally, I think it's extremely, extremely important that we as an organization have the capacity and the culture of transformation. The days of five year plans and 10 years plans are gone. Things are changing so rapidly, even the one year plans are no longer relevant. You have to update your plan already less than six months. And we can address that only because if The reset humanitarian system has both culture and capacity of transformation. And that humility I talked about before, changing or accepting the weakness is not a wrong thing. It's not a weakness, actually, it's a strength. Only strong people, strong organization has the ability to do that. So, colleagues, we are here with different roles, experiences, and perspective, but with only one shared interest, Tom, I'm repeating you. how we can work together to better serve our humanity. If you are serious about transforming the humanitarian response, then we must be serious about shifting power, resources, and responsibility closer to the people we aim to serve. That means local, local, and local, but local with global solidarity. As local as possible, as international as necessary. So a true humanity reset from the perspective of IFRC is threefold: leading with humanity, acting with foresight, and delivering with accountability. All that comes best with local at the core. Thank you so much.

I thank the Secretary General of the IFRC for his comprehensive insights on strengthening local partnerships, enhancing accountability, leveraging emerging technologies like AI, and fostering a culture of transformation that translate humanitarian commitments into tangible action and political solutions. I would now like to turn to Ms. Amy Pope, Director General of the International Organization for Migration. Amy, what would a truly reset humanitarian system look and feel like for people affected by crisis and what immediate meaningful changes should they experience first? What specific commitments can each organization make to help realize that vision and ensure the system is more effective, coherent and accountable for those it serves? Over to you.

Thank you so much, Madam Vice President. And it's wonderful to be here on this panel with some good friends and community leaders and heads of agencies. Thank you so much. First of all, I just want to state what I think is the obvious, which is that the humanitarian system today is facing immense risks. Obviously, we're seeing raging conflict. We're seeing violence around the world. We're seeing prolonged crises that are lasting for years upon years. We're seeing record displacement and displacement that is increasingly being caused by flood, by drought, by storms, and by other disasters. And we're seeing a global political system that is undergoing massive change. And there's one more risk. And I say this a bit provocatively, because that one more risk is ourselves. And when I say ourselves, I don't just mean the UN agencies and the international NGOs. I mean all of you. I mean our member states. I want to start by underscoring something that something that Yaghen said, which is that humanitarian response cannot be a substitute for the hard work of diplomacy. of ending conflict, of building stability and peace, which is necessary for the education, for the jobs, for the opportunities for people around the world. And I want to underscore that member states cannot walk away from communities in crises. cut the funding and expect that the problems are all just going to go away, that people won't then move, that young people won't then become radicalized, and that jobs will be widely available. But I also recognize that we within the UN family and within the humanitarian system have our own responsibilities. And this can't be just about creating new boxes and beautiful PowerPoints and suggesting we've done a good job and we'll see you next time. In fact, our goal must be to set aside our egos, to set aside the turf battles, and to make sure that we are focused on transforming the experience of people who need our help in ways that are relevant to their needs and not for the long term. Now, I want to share an example which has powerfully affected me. In 2024, I had the chance to go to Goma, to the Democratic Republic of Congo. And often when I travel, I'll sit down with groups of women because we know that women and girls will often have very unique experiences. And I met this one young woman who told me that at the time of the crisis, when she'd been forced to leave her home, she had been studying for exams. And now that she found herself in a camp, all she wanted were books. All she wanted was to continue her studies. But all that she was given, she told me, were birth control pills because of the high likelihood that she would be raped. Now, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this is a sign that our system is failing. This is a sign that what we are offering people is not aligned with their needs. And we know our job is not to protect what we do. We're not here to protect the humanitarian industrial complex. But we need to work together to make concrete commitments that address these gaps and address the inefficiencies. But again, I'm putting some responsibility back to all our member states. This means that you need to be with us and you need to fund it. It means you're not just funding the sexy, highly visible conflicts. It means that you also need to fund the vulnerable and you need to fund their transition. Now, I speak to hundreds of migrants and displaced people every year, and I promise you There is not one person I have ever met who says, "I love living in this camp. Please, can I stay longer?" Not one. And not one of them cares about our mandates. Not one of them cares about what vest I'm wearing or what insignia is on the back of my jacket. They just care about getting help, being safe, and having a chance to get out and to succeed. And I tell you, it starts with addressing what is increasingly a false divide between the humanitarian and the development. That's why we within IOM are we've agreed to champion the Secretary General's action plan on solutions with our partners at UNHCR, with our partners at UNDP, and with the leadership of OCHA. We have agreed that from the beginning of a conflict, we will go in with a mindset to transitioning people away from humanitarian towards solutions as quickly as possible. And there's some good examples out there. In Nigeria, the state governors are already demonstrating political will and local ownership by putting their own resources into the mix, by bringing their own money to help support displaced communities. And in Somalia, we're seeing local communities partner with the private sector so they can create new solutions for displaced people. So if we want to reset the system, we have to reset the incentives to move people off of humanitarian assistance, out of camps, and into the futures that they deserve and that they want. I had one government tell me, and they're not the only government that feels this way, that they feel that they are punished financially because they help displaced people integrate into new communities, rather than forcing them into high visibility, high fundraising potential camps. And the fact that some of these camps have been in place for decades should be seen by all of us as a failure to do this well. But that's what our fundraising system prioritizes. We raise money off of crises and dramatic stories. It doesn't prioritize raising money to solve the long-term problems, to give people the skills they need and the access to the jobs that are available. And a reset system would also ask you, our donors, our members, to share the risks. Perfect cannot be the enemy of the good. We know there is a major risk that we all share when we're empowering local actors. So let's work with them so they can manage funds effectively and responsibly. And we gotta get out of our own bubble. I've been in so many rooms where people will label, "Oh, that's a humanitarian. Oh, she doesn't understand 'cause she's not a humanitarian. She does da, da, da, da. That is a not helpful way of dividing the world and approaching the issues. We have to think broadly about who is a partner here. In our world, the diaspora is a key partner. In fact, we'll be busy trying to figure out our own solutions and raising money, and the diaspora is way ahead of us providing resources, providing a lifeline to communities who are in need. It also means Looking at partners we don't always bring to the table. The faith community, civic leaders, and of course the private sector. The private sector has everything to gain where we stabilize communities that are in crisis. So let's bring those technology companies who work with us on advanced data solutions, who will enable us to use what they do so well, deliver quickly and efficiently into the work we do in the humanitarian space, which means we need to get out of the 1990s and into 2025 and use both AI and analytics that are now available to companies around the world. And finally, real reform, it means that we have to stay true to our principles, the principles of humanitarian law, of international protection, the protection of human rights. We cannot do any of that if our first impulse is to protect our turf. We need creative, collective action. We need to focus on new incentives. We need to help people in the long term in efficient and effective ways. And our organizations, we are well positioned to truly meet this crisis head on and at scale. And now the world is asking us to take on the issue of reform head on and at scale, and we are up to the challenge. We will serve those who need us most, but we can't do it alone. We need every single one of you in this room. I don't care if you're a donor, I don't care if you're a member state or you're a member of civil society. We need every single one of you in this room to join us to serve the world's most vulnerable. So thank you very much.

I thank the Director General of IOM for asserting that the humanitarian response cannot substitute for diplomacy. Member states cannot abandon communities in crisis, leaving the largest generation of youth in history vulnerable to radicalization. We must set aside turf battles, stay true to our principles, align with the needs of those we serve, and work together to address gaps and inefficiencies while ensuring Member States fund both the vulnerable and their transitions into the future. I would now like to turn to Ms. Kelly Clements, Deputy High Commissioner for Refugees. Kelly. Current humanitarian coordination mechanisms are buckling under the weight of protracted complex crisis. What new leadership models or decision-making structures should we be piloting now? And what authority and roles are we willing to delegate and recognize to make them work?

Thank you. Thank you very much, Madam Vice President, and greetings to everyone in the room. It's really a privilege to be on this panel. And before I start talking about coordination and leadership models, yes, yes, yes. wholeheartedly agree with what my fellow panelists have already offered this morning. It's the time, it's the moment. Yesterday, we opened our UNHCR Standing Committee, and I recognized some faces in the room who were there yesterday with us. And some of that, the crisis of the moment, Madam Vice President, was as palpable there as it is this morning. and with what the President of ECOSOC said, along with the Emergency Relief Coordinator and yourselves, this is the time for this conversation. We don't have more time to waste. And I think to get to the point that the Director General, my friend Amy, said, it is something that we need to do, must do, but we have to do it with all of you. The system is overstretched. It's underfunded. And it is operating in an increasingly hostile environment, which we also heard from some of our eloquent speakers earlier today. As Tom said, it's time to regroup, to reform, and create the space for renewal. And we can do it, again, with you. We put out one of our flagship reports last week. the Global Trends Report, which talks about forced displacement around the world. Many of you have seen it. You've asked us questions about it. You know what its contents are, and none of it surprised you. We are still at record levels of people on the move for war, conflict, persecution, and other issues. Sudan, unfortunately, surpassed Syria as the largest displacement crisis globally, with 14.3 million people uprooted. A staggering figure that continues to rise, despite something that perhaps was not read as closely in that same report, that we had 10 million returns last year, 10 million returns. 1.6 million refugees, which is the highest return figure in over 20 years. That's a very sad statistic, but I think with what you've heard on the panel this morning, with the lack of political solutions, not surprising. And the resources on which we depend to be able to respond are just not keeping pace, which is why, of course, this reset is so important. We support it fully. We support the drive to reduce duplication and bureaucracy, not just to streamline for its own sake, but to shift energy and shift resources to what matters most to deliver protection and aid more effectively to people in need. In line with Tom's call, this means being bold in rethinking what we do, how we do it, and who should lead. Now, to get to what many outside this room would not spend one moment of their day or night thinking about, which is clusters, it means simplification. And of course, we fully, fully subscribe to collapsing a reduction of clusters from 11 to 8. And if you want to know more about those configurations, we'll be available at the lunch break, and we can talk about those. I do want to reassure, because one place where we take particular leadership is on the global protection cluster, and there's been a lot of discussion about whether we're going to lose very key focus of our work on gender-based violence, on child protection, on other areas that have had more visibility in previous structures. The answer to that is no, we will not. Those same voices, those same experts, those same mandates of other agencies to bring that expertise forward will be visible and will be present where it matters most, which is in these operational contexts. But we also have to bear in mind that there isn't going to be a cookie cutter approach. There's not going to be a one size fits all approach to the way that we organize ourselves at the operational level. Another source of conversation, as we've been talking about the reset, has been the refugee coordination model. This was something that the Tom's predecessor's predecessor and our High Commissioner's predecessor talked quite a bit about quite some time ago, and we refreshed the refugee coordination model last year to make it fit for purpose. Now, this doesn't mean that that needs to be the model used in every context, and one of the things that we have certainly committed together with OCHA and with under the emergency relief coordinators leadership is to look at those 16 areas where we are have mixed coordination mechanisms where there may be internal displacement with refugees, and how do we review those countries and those contexts and make sure that our coordination systems lash up, that they align, that in some cases they are integrated, or in some cases one replaces the other, and we are committed to do that in places from Ethiopia to Colombia. The issues related to coordination and coordination itself, we always have to do this. And then coming back to Amy's point that this we have to do it in close partnership with humanitarian and development actors and in different contexts. And this is where we see some differences now with what we talk about in humanitarian context, with the broader context that Amy described on the solution side. And this we cannot lose sight of. Some of those mixed situations, we've also found models that work. And here I want to come to the one that IOM and UNHCR champion, and that is related to Venezuelans in the Americas. And they do hold potential for other situations. Now, when it comes to leadership. Coordination reforms also have to be matched with robust leadership models. No one would question that. It's key. Not only individual leadership, however, but shared leadership, models that are flexible, grounded in comparative advantage, as was said earlier, and responsive to those diverse operational contexts. As you mentioned in your question, Madam Vice President, we also must be ready to delegate to trust one another's mandates and roles, to work towards coordination models that serve people, not structures. And at the country level, humanitarian and resident coordinators play, of course, a vital role in leading, convening, steering collective action while preserving the space for agencies to deliver on their own specific mandates and accountabilities. And this balance is really essential, especially in those complex and those protracted settings. where refugee and displacement dynamics are often at risk of being overlooked. The leadership of RCs and HCs, which has also been a discussion point very intensively over the last weeks and months, must be supported with the political backing of all of us, of course, but also at the country level and by all of you, and the tools to build inclusive and accountable responses. Now, a lot of discussion has already taken place this morning on what is near and dear to all of our hearts, and that is localization. We heard powerful words this morning in the opening session, including from Safi, who said it is something in terms of the leadership that we provide that needs to be reinforced. not as recipients, but as responders and leaders. And we could not agree more. We need to be simpler and we need to be lighter. We need to do more to be accountable to the people we serve, and we need to follow, to get to Yagen's point, and include them much more than we do now. This reset is an opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to local engagement. local decision-making, and indeed, local power. And we've heard the emergency relief coordinators say this before. What power do we have and what power can we share? Which leads me to the final point, which is on financing. While all of our partners have been affected by drastic funding reductions, we have made a deliberate effort to protect funding to local actors. funding to national NGOs and community-based organizations, regardless of what the funding situation looks like. We've prioritized local actors. I think when it comes to the commitment that IFRC has made to put 75% into local actors, right now we're at 85%. I hope we can keep it there and also at the same levels, but this is something that we share in terms of that kind of commitment. Processes can be burdensome for under-resourced partners, and we need to do better. And all this to just to conclude on efficiency. Efficiency has been the watchword and in some quarters has been seen as the solution. And unfortunately, no amount of reform will on its own, reverse the growing gap between humanitarian need and available funding. Our efficiency actions, of course, are not a panacea for the growing gap, but we have to do more on this too. And you've got the commitment to all of us, whether it's in UN80, it is in the IASC in terms of the humanitarian reset, it's in our own agencies. We have a very, very firm focus on these broader reforms, shared platforms, shared data, shared assessment, shared ways of being able to communicate with you, needs, impact, and so on, and we have to do much, much more. So, Madam Vice President, thank you very much for the opportunity to be able to share a few reflections. We look forward to what's to come, and more importantly, we look forward to your continued support and your commitment, because the stakes are just too high to fail. Thank you.

I thank the Deputy High Commissioner for Refugees. As you said, time is of the essence. The lack of political solutions and resources that are not keeping pace with needs underscore the urgency of the reset. We must reduce duplication, shift focus to what matters most, and be bold in thinking, rethinking our approach. This means simplification, reducing clusters, and bringing expertise forward where it matters the most. Close partnership with humanitarian and development actors is essential. Leadership coordination reforms must be matched with robust leadership models that embrace shared leadership at the local level and with the agency funds and programs with the RC system at the center. I would now like to turn to Ms. Reena Kelani, Chief Executive Officer of Plan International. As an NGO that works specifically with children, what do you want to see from the humanitarian reset? What are the challenges you see?

Thank you. Thank you, Madam Vice President. And thank you to the incredible speakers. I mean, coming at the end, you have a disadvantage, but you also have an advantage. You can complement by plagiarizing the key points that you completely agree with. And so here I'm going to talk about it from the perspective of an international NGO. Plan works in both humanitarian and development, and we're focused on children, particularly girls and youth. And so from that angle, I want to draw out some of the things that my colleagues actually have said on the panel that I think from a child's lens would have the most impact in the reset. And I just want to say how we fully support the emergency relief coordinator's leadership in this and the vision that he's laid out. Firstly, we talk a lot about marginalized communities and people at the center. What does that actually mean, and I think Yagun and others have said it. It actually means starting with listening to what they're asking us for and then acting on that. And the system as it's currently built is not built to do that. Humanitarians, I've been a humanitarian for many years and worked alongside many of you, and I'm really proud to say that we try, but the actual system, including all of us in this room, have not made it fully possible to envisage what we all want. And let me just give an example. The first thing that you hear or you talk to communities about is what they've gone through and then what do they need. And they will always put education in the first three. People are thinking about what they need today to survive, but everyone is always thinking about what is possible tomorrow. And education, as we know, it is not just about providing a structure for children in a chaotic world that they cannot understand anymore. It is protection. It gives them something to look forward to, but it also gives them protection from armed groups, from trafficking, from violence against girls. It is an essential part of the humanitarian response. And yet, education specialists are always one of the last on the truck that goes from capital Um, funding, only 10% of education in any country, and that's at the top, is ever, um, I think we've had one, Bangladesh, where we really insisted, which was a little bit more, but it's always under 10% is funded. And so we do not prioritize what we are being told is important. The other structural issue is the way we coordinate. You cannot direct this from capitals. It needs to be locally done. And there, the discussions are around how we improve coordination and streamline. The important reason to look at our coordination structure is to make sure that we reach people with what they want as well. It's not only about efficiencies. The second area, I just, sorry, just to highlight protection, one in five girls in a humanitarian context is raped. And we've all talked about it. They have experienced sexual violence, and yet protection for girls is only ever funded at 1%. There are complete structural barriers to this that today we need to have serious conversations about how to undo and fix. I want to talk about locally led action, we've all spoken about it. But from a perspective of an NGO where we work very much with local actors, whether they be youth-led groups, women's groups, local government and other local actors, this is key now. There's a lot of barriers, there's a lot of reasons that we come up with, with why that's difficult. It is now time to actually systematically look at those barriers. One is access to financing. We know that's an issue. We need to look at what options there are on the table to reduce that. The second is around the sharing of risk that Amy mentioned. It's a very real one, but now is the moment to really seriously discuss this issue. And there are many others. There are not enough capacity, et cetera, and it'll vary from country to country, but we now need to really look at what in five years' time the world will look like, and it will not look like what our system is today. And local-led action and local leadership is the future. One thing that we can do immediately, and I'm so proud to hear my colleagues talk about how they've protected local organizations that are at the front lines of this funding crash that we're facing. By the end of July, one UN agency has reported 50% of women-led organizations that existed yesterday will not exist. And many of us have put our financing towards the strong organizations. We've spent years working alongside these organizations. They are the leaders. We can't allow them to disappear overnight when we're already saying we're going to overload with too much. We need to protect what's there. The third area, and I only have four, so we can make sure that I keep it short, but the third area I want to talk to, and I'm going to paraphrase an NGO colleague of mine, is making sure that we have a resilient humanitarian ecosystem that focuses on impact. There's a lot of discussions about efficiencies, and we're all doing what we have to do and we need to do. My organization, like everyone else here, is looking at how to stop duplications, redundancies. We're looking very much at technology and how we move forward in a cost-effective way, all to make sure that most of the money that we are given goes to local-led action or to the local communities that we are there to serve. I will say that partnerships, structural reform is always complicated, but there is so much that my colleagues have talked about that we will do. Our unique advantages coming together in partnership, and we as an NGO are in discussions with several NGOs on how we actually share our resources, how when one is better at one thing, we come in and complement what they do, How if they're in one country and servicing, we don't necessarily need to do it. Perhaps we support what they're doing. Those active discussions are happening now. They're not easy, but there are some very simple things we can certainly move forward and go to our financiers as coalitions. And in terms of a resilient ecosystem, everyone's referred to it. This ecosystem exists of the UN, international NGOs, locally led actors, and even at times, you know, there are government institutions that that need to be considered. Every part of that ecosystem needs to be part of the thinking on the reset and included as as an actor. We all have complementary roles to play, and we need to make sure we factor that in as we reset the system. And lastly, Madam Vice-President, I just want to go back to what all my colleagues started with or ended with, and that is the issue of holding the line on international humanitarian law. And I'm really proud of recent statements that my United Nations colleagues have made and that they have been very forceful in red lines. There are red lines. But it requires all of us. And there's nothing in the humanitarian system that we're going to fix, that we're going to be better at, that we're going to deliver more of, that is ever going to fix the fundamental problem. And this is a political crisis that we have. We, on our part, are learning how to speak better. We're not talking in echo chambers anymore. I've seen a lot of the narrative come out explaining to people who don't understand us what we're talking about, and we will help support to do that. So thank you. And I just, I want to bring it back to the children that my organization exists for the reason we exist. If today we don't get this right, child's rights today that are at risk means that tomorrow stability, peace, security is at risk. So thank you. And I look forward to the conversation.

I thank the Chief Executive Officer of Plan International for her remarks. Rina has told us that education in humanitarian context isn't just about providing structure to children in chaotic situations. It's about protection from our groups and fostering agency. And this cannot be directed from capitals. It must be locally led. She also reminded us to stress that one in five girls in humanitarian context faces sexual violence. Local leadership is the future and we must protect women-led organizations, share resources and complement our efforts. We will now hear from the discussants for this panel who will react to what we just heard and share their assessment on current challenges to the humanitarian landscape and solutions. I now would like to turn to His Excellency, Dominic Stillhart, Ambassador and Head of Humanitarian Aid at the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, SDC, for your reflections and remarks. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Ms. Vice President, Excellencies, colleagues, distinguished panelists. And very importantly, dear Noor, Amjad and Sahar, thank you very much for being with us today. Let me start with a simple question. Why are we here? What is humanitarianism truly about? It is about people. It is about engaging with communities. And it is about the value of humanity. And yet, too often, the international humanitarian system becomes preoccupied with itself. We have seen many reform agendas and promising initiatives, especially in response to the current funding crisis. But instead of transforming our approach, we repeatedly fall back into familiar patterns of talking reform and doing more of the same. If we are serious about change and putting people at the center, we must give up something, as Ambassador Ray told us so eloquently this morning. We must let go of power and control. To be very practical, what does that mean? How do we go about this? It means building humanitarian responses around people's priorities, not institutional blueprints. It means working from the ground up, not from top down. Simple in principle, but difficult in practice, as we all know. And yet, this approach must shape every stage of the humanitarian cycle, planning, implementation and accountability. On planning, humanitarian response planning must go beyond participation. It must be localized, pragmatic and driven by context. We need a simplified humanitarian program cycle focused on protection outcomes and grounded in the priorities of affected communities. And again, I've heard a lot of agreement around some of these principles, but how do we actually get there? I think that is the question that we need to ask ourselves. By drastically reducing the complexity, if not abolish the cluster system, I'm not convinced that the reduction from 11 to 8 clusters is going to do the trick, unless clusters are not rolled out everywhere by default. And we apply, as both you, Tom, and Jagan, you said again today, we apply the principle of as local as possible and as international as necessary. We also need to shift operational planning to regional and local levels. Local actors should not just be consulted, they must lead the response. Second, on implementation, humanitarian coordinators must have significantly more oversight of programming decisions, funding flows and managed pooled funds effectively. That also puts responsibility on us as donors. We must channel significantly more funding through pooled funds, including country-based, uh, pooled funds. But even more importantly, local actors must have direct and predictable access to funding. They cannot just be implementing partners of the international system. We would like to see at least 70% of country-based pool funds go directly to local organizations. And we donors, we must learn to engage directly with civil society-led pool funds that start emerging everywhere. Third, on accountability, listening once is not enough. Accountability means continuous dialogue with those we serve at every stage. Let us make national civil society boards and community-led assessments standard practice. These mechanisms should inform humanitarian coordinated decision-making on an ongoing basis, not just during planning cycles. And finally, We need to nurture an enabling ecosystem. To localize planning, shift power in implementation and embed accountability, we need strong enabling ecosystems. That means not only clear policy commitments, but also platforms that foster trust, coordination and shared learning. Here in Geneva, we are part of such an ecosystem. This city may not be the center of humanitarian response, but it is the central backbone of humanitarian action. With its unique concentration of operational agencies, diplomatic missions, legal expertise, and multilateral networks, Geneva supports what happens on the ground. From access negotiations and anticipatory tools to reliable data and inclusive dialogue. The goal is not to centralize, but to support a system in which global capacities complement local leadership. Ultimately, we must trust. Trust in local leadership, trust in the communities we serve, and most of all, trust in humanity. So let me close where I began. How do we bring humanity back to the center of humanitarian action? By shifting power, by staying grounded, and by remembering for who we work. Thank you very much.

I thank the head of humanitarian aid at the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation for his comments and questions. I now turn to Mr. Poposki, Director General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, ECHO. Director General Poposki, thank you for being with us today. From a donor perspective, which are the most immediate and transformative reforms actions and what bold leadership decisions are needed to make that humanitarian reset vision a reality?

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. An inclusive, sustainable, and truly transformative humanitarian reset should be strongly rooted in the respect of international humanitarian and human rights law, humanitarian principles, and the centrality of protection and values of solidarity, humanity, and equality. As we see in many of today's crises, there is alarming violations of international humanitarian law, threatening not only those trapped in conflict, but the efficiency and effectiveness of humanitarian response. As donors, our role must be to reinforce adherence to the international humanitarian law by supporting robust monitoring accountability mechanism and diplomacy aimed at securing respect for humanitarian norms. We must also empower humanitarian actors to operate safely and ensure that assistance reaches civilians impartially without discrimination and without being hindered by political or military agendas. Bold actions need to be taken to reform the humanitarian coordination Impartial, independent, cross-sectoral and people-centered needs assessments lie at the heart of effective coordination. Without an accurate and timely understanding of what affected populations need and where those needs are the greatest, the response risks being inefficient or even harmful. That requires strong, impartial, independent leaders with sound humanitarian experience, those who are able to foster trust and collaboration among diverse stakeholders, including donors and governments, international agencies, local organizations, and crucially, the communities affected by crisis. True leadership is inclusive, transparent, and accountable. It elevates local voices, integrates the knowledge into planning and decision making, and values collaboration over competition. In an increasingly complex and fragmented humanitarian Landscape where crisis overlap and resources are stretched, concerted action is, is needed to advance on the efficiency agenda. This means investing in locally led responses, prioritizing in innovative funding mechanisms that can effectively deliver humanitarian assistance such as, uh, quality, efficient, accountable, multipurpose cash assistance, harnessing the transformative impact, um, of strategic supply chains. and the, um, and the sharing or pooling of, of services and operational enablers. Enhancing the efficiency of humanitarian action demands both leadership commitment to coordinate efforts that combine short term relief with long term development and peace initiatives to ensure that humanitarian aid is a foundation for, uh, future resilience, fragile context highlight the urgency of this integrated approach and the need to strengthen coordination, uh, with other stakeholders, including financial institutions, private sector, and local actors, thank you very much.

I thank the Director General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, ECHO, for his comments and questions. I now give the floor to Her Excellency Fancy Kipchek Moi, Permanent Representative of Kenya to the United Nations Office at Geneva, for her reflections. Excellency, the floor is yours.

Thank you so much. Vice President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I'm very pleased to join you at this dialogue and to share our reflection on the ongoing humanitarian reset. This also complements Kenya's engagement on the topic here in Geneva, and thank you for inviting us. I'd like to share some five points. The first one is the objective of humanitarian action must be clear. The essence of a humanitarian action, which is to save lives, must always be very clear to all actors involved. That clarity of objective must then guide engagements, processes, budgetary allocations, designation of actors, timelines, and partnerships. The objective on saving lives must supersede a focus on perpetrating a system. The second point is Actually, in tandem with what one of the panelists already said, it was Kelly Clement who said there's need to focus on the context specific. The specific context ought to guide the kind of humanitarian action taken. While lessons may be borrowed from one setting to another, it's crucial to adapt a response to the specific context in order to possibly amplify and have a more impactful humanitarian action. The third point that I want to really bring is the clarity on actors. I think we all appreciate that the humanitarian architecture has over the years grown quite significantly. With that evolution, it has also been a scene where multiple humanitarian actors, be they organizations or persons, large numbers may not often imply efficiency or positive transformative impact. I reset therefore must provide clarity on the aspects of humanitarian action to be undertaken and the specific actors involved. While there is an endeavor to undertake localization, there must be clarity on who a local actor is or is not. Ultimately, it's crucial to ensure that the national and local systems are strengthened to be able to cope with shocks and emergencies, particularly those with constitutional mandates to provide certain services and public goods to populations. Humanitarian action, therefore, should be with national actors and not for national actors. Alongside this is the importance of efficient leadership, coordination and action among the actors. The fourth point is the need for clarity on transition to stability. Most crises humanitarians are addressing are protracted, some of them running for more than 20 years. It's crucial that the humanitarian reset is clear on the modalities to address protracted crisis as well as emerging or new crisis. However, this distinction may at times bring blurry when new crisis take place within protracted crisis. It's nevertheless essential to map when the necessary transition from relief to development ought to be made. A lack of this transition risk prolonged, humanitarian situations, therefore increasing the fragility and entrapment in a state constantly dependent on humanitarian assistance. It's also very crucial to emphasize the temporary nature of humanitarian action to liberate communities from protracted dependence on assistance towards development and independence. My last point is actually on the issue of innovation. A humanitarian reset with innovation at its core is essential to ensure that the necessary adjustments are made as and when necessary. It ought to be a learning and adjusting engagement. This will also position the material architecture to adaptation to emerging trends. It will also strengthen its resilience to any disruptions. The material architecture must also rethink its financing models and explore alternative financing options that are less vulnerable to shocks, including political shocks. Thank you.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Kenya at the UN Office at Geneva for her remarks. I would like to turn now to our moderator, Mr. Conyn **** who will provide some brief reflection. Jeremy, the floor is yours.

Thank you so much, Ambassador. And it is really a privilege and a pleasure to be here with many wise and seasoned colleagues who've made such phenomenal points. I want to start with, I think, where many people have already touched on just the brutal difficulty of the past few months and of watching our sector be convulsed by these debilitating funding cuts and the very abrupt and reactive and sweeping reductions to core humanitarian services that that are ensuing as a result of that. And, you know, I think personally, for many of us as well, the mass layoffs of many colleagues and people that we have worked with and known for for decades and the expertise and the capacity that the sector is losing as a result of that. And it's very it's hard to be strategic under circumstances like that. And so I really commend the IASC principles for making a genuine and important effort to be strategic, to look beyond the reactive immediate question of how do we bring our bottom lines down to the resources that we now have available to us, and to kind of look beyond what is being dismantled right now towards what needs to be preserved, what needs to be protected, and ultimately what needs to be to be built. And, you know, the reality is that as a as a humanitarian sector now, we have to make very hard choices about how to do less with less. Tom, you've articulated this this goal of saving as many lives as possible with the available resources and. As we've heard from a number of the panelists, from Ambassador Stillhart, from Director General Pope, from Ambassador Wray, and from others, the success of that is not necessarily a foregone conclusion. Change is not easy, and sometimes, you know, the -- all of us collectively in this room, as Amy reminded us, can be part of the obstacle there, and we need to ensure that we are going to be part of the solution. It's very heartening to hear the alignment in these remarks on the way forward, that we must prioritize local leadership, particularly women's leadership. We must hold the line on preserving international humanitarian law, humanitarian values, and humanitarian principles. And we must be quite ruthless about reform and streamlining and efficiency. I do want to just read two quotes. And I'll tell you what they're from after I've read them. Quote one, we must do better at utilizing and working alongside local structures. With nothing but good intentions, the international community descends into crises in enormous numbers and its activities too often leave the very communities we are there to help on the sidelines. We must actively strengthen, not undermine, these local actors. And we must translate good intentions into meaningful reform. The fact that we continue to struggle to turn these principles into practice demands that we set about on our shared agenda with courage and commitment to see the process through. Those are quotes from the Tsunami Evaluation Coalition report 20 years ago. As Ambassador Stillhart reminded us, these are not totally new challenges to us. And I think the question for all of us, and I think what we need to challenge ourselves on, is how will we ensure that we can make it different this time? And I think we can. And I think you're hearing a commitment, and we're seeing a commitment in the comments today towards that. I will just share a few thoughts and reflections on some things that I think we must get right so that we do not when two years from now, we do not look back and say, well, the system is 30% to 40% smaller, but otherwise, we're basically doing the same thing. How do we do that? We must take a really hard look at how money flows. And it's heartening to hear so much discussion and so much energy around local funding and around pooled funding, and particularly the convergence of those two, using a greater use of pooled funding to ensure money flows directly to local actors. I think we need to be frank with ourselves that as we As we work to shift power and as large major institutions shift power to local actors, that does mean stepping back and that may mean some further shrinking. As we go about that, it's also crucial that we don't throw out the baby with the bathwater, that what is handed over and what is shifted to local actors does not undermine the really crucial core mandates and comparative advantages of our large global humanitarian institutions. It's very important that member states and donors, all of you in this room, be part of leading this change. The challenges and the agenda that are being contemplated both through the reset and through the UN80 process will require political champions. And this is a time of great political turmoil in the world. There is not always a lot of unity on major issues, and I think we will need it here. And then I will close with just echoing what a number of other speakers have said, the importance of upholding the centrality of humanitarian principles. And I think for all of us who have worked as humanitarian practitioners, what we know is when we say the principles, Those are not a religious creed, they're not an ethical commitment, they are a tool. Humanitarian principles are a tool for delivering safe and effective aid in contested environments to those who need it. And so when we talk about upholding those, we're not upholding those simply because it is a sort of ethical right thing to do, we're upholding those because we know the damage that happens when we lose those and when we abandon those. And we are seeing many reminders of that in our world today, as we heard from some of our local civil society colleagues in the opening session. I will stop there. Thank you.

Thank you, Jeremy, for your reflections. I now open the floor for comments or questions. Delegations wishing to request the floor should indicate their intention by raising their delegation's nameplate. I would like to remind delegations to strictly observe the agreed time limits of two minutes for intervention by individual delegations. To ensure proper interpretations, delegations are asked to speak at a normal pace and to provide a written copy of their statements to the Secretariat at least two hours in advance of delivery. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia.

Vice President and all the speakers today for this. important discussion. The humanitarian system is at a critical juncture with an increasing number of protracted conflicts, more frequent and intense disasters, but fewer resources for action. We also see serious challenges for the implementation of international humanitarian law, essential for the principled, safe and effective delivery of humanitarian assistance. Meeting these challenges requires collective action. Australia welcomes the IASC's leadership of the Humanitarian Reset and supports the bold reforms proposed, particularly efforts to streamline structures that increase efficiency and better deliver for those facing the most severe humanitarian needs. Australia supports the Reset's focus on localisation and increased participation of local actors in coordination and decision-making. We see opportunity for pooled funds to increasingly support localisation, learning from the breadth of experience across existing pooled funds to achieve impact and efficiency. As a donor, Australia is committed to supporting greater use of pooled funds and multi-year flexible funding backed with robust accountability and risk management mechanisms. As the humanitarian system is reimagined, Australia emphasises the importance of inclusive humanitarian action. Our ability to reach those in most severe need in crisis and disasters is critical, both to delivering on the humanitarian principles and to improving efficiency. Australia will continue to support the meaningful participation of women, children, LGBTQIA+ people and people with disability in humanitarian action. Reform efforts should ensure no region is left behind. Australia's region, the Indo-Pacific, is home to complex displacement crises and disaster and climate risks. The Myanmar and Rohingya crises require continued international support while recognising the critical role of local humanitarian actors. Australia supports continued prioritisation of climate-responsive and preparedness initiatives in our region, including anticipatory action and early warning system, which both saves lives and reduces the costs of responding. Australia will defend the normative role of the UN to ensure access and protection for all humanitarian actors. Humanitarian and broader UN reforms must align the peace and security and development functions of the UN to address the root causes of humanitarian need. We stand ready to contribute to a streamlined and efficient humanitarian system that puts crisis-affected people at the center. Thank you.

Thank you, Vice-President. Mexico believes that the humanitarian system reform must place affected persons at the heart of response, recognising them as active protagonists of change. We express our profound concern at the growing trend towards increased human suffering in multiple armed conflict contexts currently. Given those challenges, it's crucial for humanitarian reform to advance, taking into account three key pillars. First, we agree with the proposal that humanitarian coordinators, in consultation with humanitarian country teams, review their strategies, prioritise action that saves lives and simplify structures to adapt them to each operational context. Local actors who have high knowledge of the ground as well as the trust of their communities should be at the heart of implementation. Second, we agree with the proposal that significant transformative inclusion. The system must guarantee meaningful participation of women, girls, and historically marginalized populations, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples, and IDPs throughout all humanitarian cycle stages. Third, unswerving respect for IHL and humanitarian principles. We reaffirm the importance of guaranteeing at all times, all places, security and protection for humanitarian personnel. Their work saves lives and is an essential pillar of any response. Thus, we recall that all parties to a conflict have an obligation under IHL to enable and facilitate access for them without restrictions to humanitarian assistance. Deliberately obstructing access can constitute an international crime and should be investigated and sanctioned by multilateral competent mechanisms. Mexico reiterates its commitment to humanitarian system reform, which places in the centre humanitarian principles, human dignity, bolsters local leadership and guarantees protection of those who make humanitarian assistance possible. Thank you.
